Cross-Border Vehicle Theft

By: Nicky Troll | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
HOME-INVASION, HELD HOSTAGE and your CAR STOLEN. All three contact crimes in a matter of hours. Northern KZN communities are under siege from relentless cross-border criminal syndicates feeding an in

Unique Selling Point:
** NEW CRIME TREND
** IMMERSIVE STORY TELLING
** GRIPPING CASE STUDY ACCOUNT OF TRAUMATIC CRIME

Summary:
Crime is a daily reality for South Africans. Shockingly the chances of you being a victim of contact crime in your lifetime is more likely than unlikely. But imagine being the victim of first a home invasion, then being taken hostage and then having your car stolen and being dumped in a foreign country. Yep, that’s the latest crime trend in South Africa.

Communities in Northern KZN are being hit with a hattrick of crimes perpetrated by ruthless criminal syndicates that target luxury SUVs that are high in demand a cross the border.

We head to the border to get the inside scoop on this worrying crime trend.

Further information:
CB first reported on cross border vehicle theft in 2004. In 2014, a staggering R8.5 billion worth of vehicles are stolen and hijacked in SA annually. At the time almost 30%, was taken across the border to neighbouring countries where syndicates make huge profits. Eight years later and not much has changed. Illegal vehicle crossing are still a common occurrence – the only thing that changes is the MO.
** LOOKING FOR NEWER STATS

Towards the end of 2019/2020 the trend was to lure business people to remote areas close to the border with the promise of contracts – only to steal their vehicles and leave them stranded while the cars illegally crossed the border to Mozambique.

As word got out and companies grew wise to these cunning tactics – the quotation gang’s reign was cut short and the incidents decreased.

Fast forward to 2022 and now the criminals have come up with a new MO. They break into your house, they take you hostage and drive your car to the border – once they cross over illegally, they dump you in the fields.

In the week between Christmas and New Year there were three incidents all in the Northern KZN region.

We interview one of these cases – they’ve agreed to speak to us on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution.

Mr. X was visiting his father at their farm just outside of Manguze about 17km from the Kosi Bay border line with his wife and sister.

In the early hours of 27th of December armed men broke into their home. They were woken up to threats of violence, told to get in the car in their pyjamas and driven off with.

Mr. X says they were numbed by fear, he and his father were hit with the back of a hand gun and they were constantly reminded who was in charge.

The ordeal lasted two and a half hours, they were dumped on the Mozambique side as the their Fortuner sped off into the distance.

Ironically this is not the first time, the same car had been stolen – in February the vehicle was also taken a cross the border, but it was recovered, sadly only to be stolen 11 months again – but this time the trauma was beyond they could ever have imagined.

Mr. X speaks really well and is adamant that real action needs to be taken – as it seems that this isn’t a priority for government to get a grip on.

WHAT IS GOVERNMENT DOING
Over the years securing the border has gone from being the police’s responsibility to becoming the mandate of the SANDF. Today private security companies do most of the cross border recoveries along the porous border line.

WHAT BORDER LINE?
Well as in most cases along the borders of South Africa a filmsy fence is all that stands between criminals and the movement of illicit goods and stolen vehicles, it’s not a deterrent but rather an indication of where the borderline sits.

In 2020 an R85 million rand concrete jersey fence projected kicked off – it looked like the 1.5 meter concrete wall like structure would be the solution and end the non-stop illegal activity along the hardest hit 8km stretch of border between South African and Mozambique in northern KZN. But alas, while R48 million was paid, only 100 meters of the project was completed in June 2021 when the it was halted became the focus of a SIU investigation that is yet to be completed.

CHARACTERS
** INFORMANT – We speak to a fence cutter who is a scout for the drivers – clearing the route and making sure there is an easy crossing point for the cars when the come charging through

** SECURITY COMPANY – We speak to Pierre Conradie who runs an independent security company in the region and does recoveries – he will go with us to the border, explain the challenges and the modus operandi’s.

** EXPERT – Tinus Odendal from IAATI The International Association of Auto Theft Investigators will give us an overview of cross border vehicle trends, discuss the demand and supply and the importance of curbing vehicle theft. (zoom interview with the border in the background – hopefully)

** COMMUNITY VOICE – Judas Mthembu is from an organisation against crime – he represents the local community – he works closely with the police and security companies and will give us an understanding of the impact on the community and how widespread it is.

TREATMENT
Gritty, on the ground, filming in situ telling the story in an immersive style. We’ll get drone footage as well and try and do interesting links.

Presenter for a three days, travel – flight and accommodation for crew.

STRUCTURE

UPSOUND FROM RE-ENACTMENT 7 seconds

VICTIM: They broke the door open //they barged in // they held us at gunpoint.

VO: This may feel like just another home invasion, but it’s a home invasion with a twist - this story is about cars.

BREATHER…. 3 seconds

Vehicle theft in South Africa is an epidemic. Relentless……. Ruthless…… And on the rise.

BREATHER…. 3 seconds upsound – open your, open your car…

LINK: On average 50 cars are hijacked every single day in the country. That’s 50 vehicles taken by force every single day across South Africa.

TINUS: A stolen vehicle or hijacked vehicle //is one of the primary enablers of serious crime.

VO: Tinus Odendal is from the International Association Of Auto Theft Investigators.

At least a quarter of stolen cars head illegally to neighbouring countries - that’s billions of rands lost to the black market.

TINUS: It's not only the vehicles. This will show huge demand for parts, spare parts.

VO: Cars cross either through the border post with fraudulent paperwork and possibly a liberal greasing of palms. Or – more blatantly through the actual fence.

TINUS: It's an industry, and they also mitigate risk. / they change modus operandi,

VIO: As technology advances, criminals adapt.

Simply stealing a modern car is near impossible with heightened security features and tracking companies on standby. This means criminals don’t just need the car and the key – they now need the vehicle owner as well.

A trend that has spiked in areas close to borders – particularly in Northern KwaZulu Natal.

PIERRE: The reason is to get that vehicle across the border as quickly as possible, And it also prevents the owner then from notifying the authorities

VO: Pierre Conradie heads a local security firm in the region - he’s says the violence has escalated.

In the last week of December there were three incidents just days apart - all within 20 km from the border.

This 40 year old professional was attacked in his family home by a cross border syndicate.

VICTIM: In the area where we are there,// when somebody breaks into your property at those early hours of the morning, then you know, that's all they want is what you parked outside.

LINK: It’s all about supply and demand and meeting your customers’ needs – even when it comes to the international black market for luxury cars - criminal syndicates are so brazen that they don’t steal cars randomly – they steal on order.

PIERRE: They steal on demand, and they steal on colour, they will even steal on what type of rim they want on that side. The vehicle that goes across the border, not that's not the baseline vehicle. It’s expensive vehicles, six, seven, eight and a thousand plus vehicles, that goes to the market

BREATHER…. 3 seconds

VO: These gangs come armed and aggressive under the cover of darkness.

BREATHER…. 3 seconds

VICTIM: They tied us up // they demanded guns, money. We were scared and terrified.

VO: Still in pyjamas, he was forced into his SUV with his fiancé, sister and father. As the car sped off they were numbed by fear as they drove towards the border line.

VICTIM: they were just making phone calls and calling their counterparts, checking if the roads was clear.

TOM: Suspects will use routes like this through these densely forested areas at night.

VO: Tom is from a local vehicle recovery ground team - having worked in the area for close to a decade, he’s recovered more than 500 cars.

TOM: At night time, they use these forests as cover to get as close to the border as possible. And then they break cover across the border. Vehicles gone

VO: Once the vehicles leave South Africa, the chances of getting the car back diminish significantly.

TINUS: The moment it crosses the border, you start working with different legislation, language barriers, and the process // Just to get it back can be very expensive.

VO: In some instances, so-called insiders in cross border syndicates try to extort the vehicle owners.

TINUS: You will get a call saying that your vehicle is recovered and if you pay X amount, //they will tell you we it is// but the majority, the majority is a scam where the moment you deposited the money, your informant is gone.

VO: There are no hard and fast rules when it comes to cross border theft – the goal is always the same - get it over the border. FAST.

PIERRE: This is a well-organized, well-orchestrated operation that's run by syndicates, // with big money behind it. There's a lot of people that's got a that's holding a hand.

VO: The gunmen get the wheels to the jockeys, who drive on routes that scouts have checked out, through the borderline that’s been cut by fence cutters.

We reached an informant by phone. He is a fence cutter. He works regularly. And even at his level in the syndicate makes good money.

INFORMANT: One car, maybe R3000, sometimes R2000 - maybe a week - three or four. // it is easy money, even though it’s dangerous – but, it comes our way.

LINK: This is the fence dividing South Africa and Mozambique – it’s not a deterrent but rather an indication of where the borderline sits.

VICTIM: The fence that you have for your own house, it's better than the fence that we have to protect the country between these two countries

VO: We joined Tom on a patrol along the fence. While there was a military presence, there were stretches of unmanned borderline.

CLAIRE: We just saw some tyre tracks going into a freshly built fence, it looks like. Are there people that are crossing the border here illegally?
TOM: // at this point in time is we're losing between 12 and 15 vehicles a month. Gone through the fence on my right. You could actually just walk up to it and push it over if you wanted to.
CLAIRE: WOW

VO: We stopped at a recent crossing point.

TOM: They run through the border. You can actually still see all tyre tracks here,M11 // // You can still see it on the impressions on the grass over there. This is probably about five or six days ago at this cross. You can see the SANDF guys are trying to //block these vehicles crossing. //
CLAIRE: because this is so easily removable and they can just cut the fence again,
TOM: correct again. Fences being repaired, cut, cut, cut, cut, cut, cut, cut. There you go.
CLAIRE: Literal pieces of the fence.

VO: It’s hardly a labour intensive job - the fence is cut and the car crosses over quickly.

INFORMANT: It’s only takes two minutes – the car is already waiting in the bush.// it will never stop – it’s too easy to stop. it can happen sometimes that two cars can come, one in the afternoon and another in the morning

VO: Victims are taken across as well and dumped on the other side of the fence, a short distance into Mozambique - usually their freedom comes with a threat of violence.

VICTIM: The promise that those guys made when they released us don't dare try to follow up on this vehicle, I would come back and shoot you. So those words to me, they mean they meant death.

VO: They made their way to a homestead nearby - in a matter of hours, they had been victims of three contact crimes - a home-invasion, held hostage and their car stolen.

VICTIM: every night you are living in fear because you don't know what's next. there's a lot that needs to be done. The law enforcement locally, they cannot conquer these things on their own.

VO: The local community has stepped in and is getting involved with crime prevention operations. Juda Mthethwa, represents the Umhlabuyalingana Society Against Crime.

JUDA: We don't deny that the government is helping us, but there is no change .

VO: Mthetwa comments that while the local police, priority crime investigators, the military, and community groups appear to be trying to combat this crime scourge - the positive results are yet to be seen and the local community is frustrated.

JUDA : You ask yourself why are people crying while there are all these structures? And we are failing, all of us? This thing is a recurring, recurring. No, no, no, something’s fishy, something’s fishy.

VO: There is a lot of distrust in law enforcement and even within the community - Mthetwa admits, locals have been roped in by the criminals and are profiting from crime.

JUDA: They leave the school and go and cut the fence. They think that it is a job, just to do that, failing understand that they are torturing their community.

VO: It’s an easy job according to the fence cutter - you just need to find a gap in the soldiers patrols.

INFORMANT: We don’t pay them, we check which way they walk, I must rush, because the soldier can come any time – they are always up and down there.

VO: With the military presence clearly not enough of a deterrent, an R85 million concrete barrier was commissioned in 2020. We saw ditches meant for foundations and material just standing in the fields.

TOM: because of the corruption issue, everything's on hold.
CLAIRE: So how long have these foundations been like this?
TOM: You can see this the vegetation growing on them. So that's been there for a while.

VO: The project was stopped in 2021 by the Special Investigating Unit.

CLAIRE: So do you think if this was running the entire length of the border, it would stop or completely eliminate cross-border vehicle drift?
TOM: It won't completely eliminate it, but it will be a significant advantage to us. But these guys are clever. They have already found a way to get over,
CLAIRE: The Get over this.
TOM: It has happened
CLAIRE: HOW?
TOM: They construct a ramp and they basically drive the vehicle up the ramp on one side of the ramp on the other side.

VO: These images were taken in October 2021 - while it was an ambitious approach - the car thieves were not successful and set the vehicle alight.

It appears the current law enforcement interventions are not working, Conradie believes the region requires a unique solution, specific to the area.

PIERRE: This is Zulu land, it's not Disneyland, it's frustrating for us because something can be done about it. We've got the equipment. We've got the technology to assist in fighting this crime. I just think the coordinated effect, the effort is not there.

VO: But until then, South Africans will continue to be preyed on by callous criminals who feed the lucrative cross border market.

VICTIM: It's not the first time happening to me, and it's not the last time I know if it still carries on like this with that kind of fence, with this kind of law enforcement, it's going to go on. It's going to go on and on and on and on.

VO: We investigate how contact crimes in northern Kwazulu Natal are evolving

We head to the border with Mozambique and make some startling discoveries.

VO: Patchy communication systems, vast distances and infiltrated law enforcement networks add fuel to a raging car theft trend where vehicle owners are taken hostage across . 11 seconds

You can see the SANDF guys are trying to //block these vehicles crossing. // CLAIRE: because this is so easily removable and they can just cut the fence again, TOM: correct again. INFORMANT: It’s only takes two minutes – the car is already waiting in the bush.// it will never stop – it’s too easy to stop. it can happen sometimes that two cars can come, one in the afternoon and another in the morning VO: Victims are taken across as well and dumped on the other side of the fence, a short distance into Mozambique - usually their freedom comes with a threat of violence. VICTIM: every night you are living in fear because you don't know what's next. there's a lot that needs to be done. The law enforcement locally, they cannot conquer these things on their own. metadata.Unique Selling Point: ** NEW CRIME TREND ** IMMERSIVE STORY TELLING ** GRIPPING CASE STUDY ACCOUNT OF TRAUMATIC CRIME
metadata.Summary: Crime is a daily reality for South Africans. Shockingly the chances of you being a victim of contact crime in your lifetime is more likely than unlikely. But imagine being the victim of first a home invasion, then being taken hostage and then having your car stolen and being dumped in a foreign country. Yep, that’s the latest crime trend in South Africa. Communities in Northern KZN are being hit with a hattrick of crimes perpetrated by ruthless criminal syndicates that target luxury SUVs that are high in demand a cross the border. We head to the border to get the inside scoop on this worrying crime trend.
metadata.Further information: CB first reported on cross border vehicle theft in 2004. In 2014, a staggering R8.5 billion worth of vehicles are stolen and hijacked in SA annually. At the time almost 30%, was taken across the border to neighbouring countries where syndicates make huge profits. Eight years later and not much has changed. Illegal vehicle crossing are still a common occurrence – the only thing that changes is the MO. ** LOOKING FOR NEWER STATS Towards the end of 2019/2020 the trend was to lure business people to remote areas close to the border with the promise of contracts – only to steal their vehicles and leave them stranded while the cars illegally crossed the border to Mozambique. As word got out and companies grew wise to these cunning tactics – the quotation gang’s reign was cut short and the incidents decreased. Fast forward to 2022 and now the criminals have come up with a new MO. They break into your house, they take you hostage and drive your car to the border – once they cross over illegally, they dump you in the fields. In the week between Christmas and New Year there were three incidents all in the Northern KZN region. We interview one of these cases – they’ve agreed to speak to us on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution. Mr. X was visiting his father at their farm just outside of Manguze about 17km from the Kosi Bay border line with his wife and sister. In the early hours of 27th of December armed men broke into their home. They were woken up to threats of violence, told to get in the car in their pyjamas and driven off with. Mr. X says they were numbed by fear, he and his father were hit with the back of a hand gun and they were constantly reminded who was in charge. The ordeal lasted two and a half hours, they were dumped on the Mozambique side as the their Fortuner sped off into the distance. Ironically this is not the first time, the same car had been stolen – in February the vehicle was also taken a cross the border, but it was recovered, sadly only to be stolen 11 months again – but this time the trauma was beyond they could ever have imagined. Mr. X speaks really well and is adamant that real action needs to be taken – as it seems that this isn’t a priority for government to get a grip on. WHAT IS GOVERNMENT DOING Over the years securing the border has gone from being the police’s responsibility to becoming the mandate of the SANDF. Today private security companies do most of the cross border recoveries along the porous border line. WHAT BORDER LINE? Well as in most cases along the borders of South Africa a filmsy fence is all that stands between criminals and the movement of illicit goods and stolen vehicles, it’s not a deterrent but rather an indication of where the borderline sits. In 2020 an R85 million rand concrete jersey fence projected kicked off – it looked like the 1.5 meter concrete wall like structure would be the solution and end the non-stop illegal activity along the hardest hit 8km stretch of border between South African and Mozambique in northern KZN. But alas, while R48 million was paid, only 100 meters of the project was completed in June 2021 when the it was halted became the focus of a SIU investigation that is yet to be completed. CHARACTERS ** INFORMANT – We speak to a fence cutter who is a scout for the drivers – clearing the route and making sure there is an easy crossing point for the cars when the come charging through ** SECURITY COMPANY – We speak to Pierre Conradie who runs an independent security company in the region and does recoveries – he will go with us to the border, explain the challenges and the modus operandi’s. ** EXPERT – Tinus Odendal from IAATI The International Association of Auto Theft Investigators will give us an overview of cross border vehicle trends, discuss the demand and supply and the importance of curbing vehicle theft. (zoom interview with the border in the background – hopefully) ** COMMUNITY VOICE – Judas Mthembu is from an organisation against crime – he represents the local community – he works closely with the police and security companies and will give us an understanding of the impact on the community and how widespread it is. TREATMENT Gritty, on the ground, filming in situ telling the story in an immersive style. We’ll get drone footage as well and try and do interesting links.
